utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to all. May we begin in the usual manner by having the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Mr. Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Case Manager Tatjana Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If there are no preliminary matters that need delay us, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this isn't going to delay you so the usher can bring the witness in. We applied for protective measures for Witness 213, who is coming next week. I understand from speaking to Mr. Krgovic there's no objection. I don't know whether anybody else has got any objection. So if we could have a decision on that, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have an objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, me neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Before I invite Ms. Korner to continue, I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, can I, this morning, before we continue with the documents in this case, just deal with two slightly separate matters. Firstly, we've seen that Mr. Cvijetic was chief of the CSB during the relevant period. Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was killed in 1993, in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And secondly, I just want to deal with the topic of intercepts very briefly. You were asked to listen to a number of intercepts, and can I just deal with them in this way:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was listed on the proofing note which was supplied to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the voice of Mico Stanisic - and don't worry about the -- the numbers I'm about to read - on intercepts which had the numbers 2695 -- 65 ter numbers 2695-1088, and 1090, on which intercept 1090 you were also able to recognise the voice of someone called Miljenko Borovcanin, and also on 1054 you recognised Mico Stanisic's voice? Can I just ask you, who is Milenko Borovcanin? Is he a relation of yours or just somebody who has the same name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko is no relation of mine. I don't know how you understood it, but in the Orthodox faith, if your patron saint is not the same -- we are not related. We just share the same last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know who he was, what position he held in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before the war, he was in the police station of Novi Grad, and during the war I believe he was assistant commander of a police station in the process of being established in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you also heard, recognised the voice of Karisik, the head of the Special Police on intercepts which were numbered 1091 and 1095. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely whom he was talking to, but I recognised his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you, sir. That's all that I want to ask you about those matters. I'm sorry, I should have asked you one further matter. Were you aware of the -- called the Serb autonomous areas, in particular the SAO Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that until later when it was reported in the media, when I understood that it was an area that the centre was covering, if I understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you never heard about anybody who was president of that Serb autonomous region or any kind of Assembly that was ever held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we return, then, please to some of the documents you looked at. Not all, you'll be happy to hear. We dealt with, although I said we were going to go back to it, I think we've done everything we need to with that, the 11th of July meeting in Belgrade. Could you have a look now, please, at 6 -- I'm sorry, Exhibit P610, which will come up on the screen again, but quite slowly, I'm afraid. This is a report on the implementation of the conclusions from the meeting of senior personnel in the MUP held on the 11th of July, and these minutes are headed "Sarajevo, August 1992." Did you see this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, we went through this document yesterday. I attended that meeting, and that implies I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I ask you to look, please, at the -- in English it's the second page, and I think it's the same in the B/C/S version. Now, it appears that the ministry had sent out a telegram on the 17th of August, asking for responses to certain questions, and this is a document issued by your CSB replying to the questions. Under item number 6, I think the question was - unfortunately we don't have the document here - about the investigation of war crimes, and here it's stated: "They have started with video cassettes on processed war crimes." War crimes against whom were being investigated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, by that time, war crimes were really being committed in an area called Birca, in the area of the police station Bratunac, and some in the area of the police station Milici. And if I remember well, a scenes of crimes officer team went out onto the scene to document these war crimes, and there are photographs. They tried to do their best to conduct a professional on-site investigation with the personnel and the inspectors that were available, so I know that for a fact those were war crimes against the Serbian population in the area of Podrinje, mainly in the municipality of Bratunac, including the village of Kravica and some other places I've forgotten. And I have to add, I'm sorry, if there had been any crimes committed by Serbs and we had known about them, I believe they would have been treated in the same way as these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've anticipated my next question. As far as you know, was any investigation carried out into war crimes committed against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that. On-site investigations were carried out. Oh, you mean against non-Serbs? At that time, you have to believe me, I was engaged in other work. It would not be good for me to answer that question without proper information and statistics. People from the crime department should be asked that question. They did their job day to day, and they had all the documents. I was engaged in operations work with uniformed police, and I spent a lot of my time in the field doing specific jobs. Without proper information, it would not be a good idea for me to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you were able to give me detail -- or give us details of the investigations in crimes into Serbs, what was alleged to be war crimes against Serbs. Are you saying that you don't know of any investigations against Muslims? Of war crimes that had taken place as against non-Serbs, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I her later that there had been a few such investigations, and I believe it's documented somewhere, but I cannot speak in a substantiated way about these things because I was not involved in those investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, during that period of 1992, were there any investigations into any of the events that had taken place, for example, in Hrasnica, Susica camp, for example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I partly answered that question yesterday when I said that when we heard about Susica, a lot of water had passed under the bridge, and I learned more about it from the media than we had official reports, because there were many incidents going on; I was in the field a lot; it was difficult to keep up with these things. I can't say I knew about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all that I want to ask you, thank you, about that document. Can we move next, please, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could I just ask a question for clarification of this, because I'm not sure I fully understood your testimony in respect of your involvement in the investigation of war crimes. You said that you were aware of the fact that the war crimes prevention service had gone out to investigate crimes in three different police stations where allegedly crimes -- war crimes had been committed against Serbs, and you told us that videos were taken and some preliminary investigations were made, and then when Ms. Korner asked you about similar war crimes committed against non-Serbs, you said that you were not involved or had no information about this. So my question is why is there a difference between your involvement in crimes against Serbs compared to crimes against non-Serbs? Or have I misunderstood your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] there's probably a misunderstanding. I said that employees of the crime department led by inspectors conducted on-site investigations into crimes against the Serb population. And that has been documented, as I said. I added later that I was sure that if there had been reports about crimes against non-Serbs, knowing my colleagues, I believe they would have treated these reports in the same way, gone out and investigated. Also, I did not participate directly in these on-site investigations, but I looked at some of the photographs, for instance, when there were massive crimes involving hundreds of victims, and I also participated myself in the investigation in a village. I believe it was called Pantici near Zvornik. I just happened to be in the field with that team. As for other reports and on-site investigations into crimes against non-Serbs, I can't say I was directly involved. But I have to say, again, I believe my colleagues were professionals and they would have dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, just to be sure, when, later on, you learned that crimes, in fact, had also been committed against non-Serbs, you heard of no investigation being made to investigate those crimes. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one unofficial informal conversation, and I believe there's even a document about it, it says that investigations had been carried out into crimes against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just continue for one moment on this theme. One of your duties was to -- to send inspectors to the various SJBs you've told us yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And one of their jobs, looking at that checklist of what they had to do, was to look at the books to see what crimes had been record and what investigations had been carry out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Every crime had to be recorded in the books that were prescribed by the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And their reports should have contained references, particularly to, for example, major killings, shouldn't they, and what was happening about the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Every serious crime, especially murder, had priority in our work above all other crimes such as theft and robbery and suchlike. I don't really understand what you're asking me. Everything was documented. Everything was processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But from what you say, you don't recall any reference in any reports to any war crimes committed in particular places against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's try to distinguish between two things. If a police inspector came to carry out an inspection at a police station, he was to inspect the internal organisation, the keeping of records, operative work, security plans, the engagement of policemen. He was to inspect solely the work of uniformed policemen. My colleagues in the crime department were much more involved in this other area of work that you're asking me about now. And I think people who were involved in that work know much more about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just but finally then, Vlasenica did come under the CSB that you were employed in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisationally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, do you want to -- to add a caveat to that? In other words, you say, "Organisationally speaking, yes." Are you trying to say that practically it didn't?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you look at the organisational scheme of the CSB, the security services centre, we looked at it yesterday, you see the head of the centre and the police stations below, that's what I mean. Organisationally, they fell under us. There's no dilemma there, that that's implied. They were under our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to pursue this any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just mention, and we should perhaps have put it in for completeness sake, the document that's referred to, the 17th of the 8th, 1992, was the request. It is actually on our 65 ter list just so it links up. So it's numbered 217, and I wish to put it in for completeness sake but just so it links. Thank you. Right. Can we move now, please, to document, continuing in the chronological fashion, 2879, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from the CSB crime prevention department to the SJBs, and we see "Vlasenica" in the second line. And it's addressed to the chief, and it's signed by somebody called Simo Tus -- Tusevljak. Sorry. There are occasions when I have serious problems. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this was a request to forward information about the period from the 1st of April to the 30th of July about crimes, and did you know about this -- this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As in the CSB, we held regular working collegium meetings, and each department chief would brief the head about the priority tasks that lay ahead. My colleague Mr. Tusevljak, in accordance with the request and the dispatch from the meeting, did this because the minister gave outstanding orders that this information should be provided to the information listed in this document. This was a professional approach to the job in those times of chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, sir. That's all I want to ask you about the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we now have, please, up P730.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do apologise. It's Exhibit P992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Can we have P730 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report to the ministry, dated the 3rd of August -- in fact, it's actually addressed to the minister himself - on the realisation of an order dated the 27th of July, 1992, and the document itself appears to be unsigned. I think that's because, in fact, part of the document is missing. But if we look at the first paragraph, it says: "Acting in accordance with your order and the working agreement with ... the CSB, I visited the majority of the public security stations in that area except for Skelani and Bratunac, which were visited, as agreed, by the chief of the police department in the CSB, Drago Borovcanin." So are you able to say, when you look at this document, who it is likely to have been written by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When going through the document with the investigator, I had a dilemma. I see that it is quite well written with quite a lot of information from the ground, and if my name wasn't mentioned here where it said I visited only Bratunac and Skelani, I might have thought I had written it myself. A colleague of mine did this very well. But I'm not sure; I don't know who did this. I can only assume it was someone from the MUP, from the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look at a couple of parts of the document, and we'll come on to the report you did next.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Firstly, it's in paragraph -- second page in English, and it's still the first page, I think, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where it says: "The majority of the public security stations in the territory of this centre established good co-operation with the units of the army of the Serbian Republic, especially in the plan of integral defence, where members of the police are filling up the crisis areas at the defence line, joint work with the military police, and so on." Now, can we pause there for a moment because I just want to ask you something about this co-operation between the military and the police. To your knowledge, did the -- were police units sent to assist the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who would be in command of the police unit that assisted the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, it was like this in those days: If we received a request from a military command that we should provide assistance in manning one of the demarcation lines, then with the approval of the ministry and the chief of the centre a dispatch would be prepared which would contain the following information: For example, we need a company of a hundred men. And then we would write to all the SJBs asking them to provide a few policemen depending on their manpower levels so that they would not be depleted too much, and the unit that would be formed in this way would be commanded by a local company leader, someone with experience, who would take that unit to the demarcation line. When this was done, he had to report to the military command in the combat zone in question. And after that, they would be resubordinate to the Army of Republika Srpska, and they would carry out their tasks jointly with the military while their shift lasted. Let me just add why it was we who appointed the company leader. We wanted to remain in contact with them, and it was their responsibility to draw up a report on what was happening, to check on the discipline of the officers on the front line, to report on any casualties, and so on. That was their task, but they were resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska in compliance with the law then in force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- you've told us who -- that the -- it would be commanded by a local company leader. In practice, what sort of rank would that company leader hold?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the minister gave that a lot of thought, and in both situations we were duty bound to have a military sort of structure so that we would know who could be a company leader, and they were people who had experience. We also looked at their military specialties that they had had in the JNA. If they had any kind of military speciality, we would take that into account. If someone had been a reserve officer, for example, in Bileca, which was a barracks that was held in high esteem where people were well trained, and we had then confidence in people who had been trained there. If they happened to be in the police, we would appoint such men to be company leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But they were still -- they were still police officers; they weren't military -- they weren't in the VRS. They were still part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were, yes, but while they were at the demarcation line, we didn't have contact with them. If anything dishonourable happened there, it would be military security that would deal with that. If there was something like a crime, God forbid, something really atrocious, we would suspend them even before they returned to the base. And, of course, disciplinary proceedings would be instituted. And as for criminal prosecution, that would be in the purview of the court. The two processes would run in parallel. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the situation if there had been a request for police assistance, as you put it, on the demarcation line. Where the situation was that in a particular area the army were operating but also obviously police were carrying out their duties, would the police there, if there were just ordinary work going on, be resubordinated to the army, or would they be responsible to their own MUP chain of command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to illustrate this with an example. Imagine a demarcation line cutting through the territories of one or more SJBs. This was the case around the city of Sarajevo where there was not a single station that was not in a combat area. If the military was active on the territory of an SJB, we had nothing to do with that. They did their work, and we did our regular work, unless they expressly asked for a squad or a company to assist them and then we would provide that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's fairly clear. All right. Can we just go back to the document for a moment. In this document at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's paragraph 3 on that -- the English page, being a special problem. In the B/C/S we need to go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Here your inspector is dealing with the paramilitary formation problem. He says: "True as I was informed, they were responding and helping the units of the Serbian Army and police, but obviously they have some special motives for war, and they don't want to put themselves under the army command," et cetera. "In some areas, for example, in Ilidza and Pale, they are staying in separate buildings and are often on the move and in different areas. On the route Sarajevo-Zvornik and in the course of leaving the field, also when leaving as a group, they make problems for the local public security stations, ignoring them or even threatening to attack the policemen at the check points. And this was recently the case with the so-called 'Carlijevci' in Vlasenica." Now, can I just ask you first of all about were you aware of the problems of paramilitaries before you -- you even saw this report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I wish they hadn't helped us. As soon as the war broke out, quite a lot of these groups arrived. They were self-organised. And there were all sorts of groups. And for you to understand this completely, in the very beginning there were groups who very well equipped with the new uniforms and they were tidy and neat so one thought they might have been trained, but very soon we came to understand that their motivation was not to help and to be active on the lines. They were a mixture of criminals, people prone to looting, and all sorts of people. So they did a lot of damage to us, and I wish they hadn't arrive. They were everywhere, especially in the Podrinje area, because Serbia was nearby and they saw it as a sort of gold mine. And they visited that area daily. I can expand on that if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, don't worry. We might -- I just want to ask you one further question about that. Are you aware of any request being made by your chief to the minister that there should be some kind of assistance from the Special Police or -- or anybody else or the army to get rid of these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't know whether they were in the composition of the military commands. There were quite a few of these renegade commands who would simply declare themselves to be some sort of unit, but in the very beginning we didn't really understand what was going on. We thought they were part of the army. And to tell you the truth, at the very beginning we were happy when helped -- when help arrived. But when we saw what their real motivation was and what their contribution was, very few of them were killed and those that were not killed in combat but during looting. I moved around in areas such as Bratunac, Skelani, Ilidza, and Sarajevo, and you asked me whether we had information and passed it on. At the collegium meetings, we continually discuss these topics. We knew these groups existed, and it was very dangerous to take any sort of thoughtless action against them. These people numbered more than a hundred in some cases. And as an experienced policeman, I thought we should talk to these people to avoid bloodshed, because I was responsible for the policemen under my command. Those were very difficult times, you know. And the way they took the bridges in the Podrinje area, for example, where they had policemen to act as a front, they were reserve policemen whom they used to conceal their smuggling activities, and it was very difficult, very difficult to get these people out of our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, this report says they were responding and helping the units of the army and police. Was that a view, as you've told us, that early on was held, that they could help the police in carrying out their duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll illustrate this with an example to help you understand. For example, Carli's men were mentioned here. They were in Sarajevo and Grbavica and Lukavica before. And in April - it was still early on - we were expecting an attack according to some security information we had, intelligence we had. And there was a leader - I've forgotten his name - they all had some sort of nicknames. And I, "Well, you're experienced. Let's act together on this line, separating the part of Sarajevo in question from Lukavica," and in the morning they called me up on a Motorola and said there was an attack, a policeman was killed. I went up there and I saw that the policeman had been hit by a piece of shrapnel from a mine, from a shell, and the police wanted to attack me. They said, "You should be ashamed of yourself. You brought these men here, but they weren't on the front line. They went to a house nearby where they gambled and spent the time there, and I saw this with my own eyes."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us there was these -- this problems was discussed at various collegiums, was Mico Stanisic present when these problems were discussed in collegiums at any stage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, all the initiative came from the minister. He wanted to create a professional MUP. He was facing a situation of chaos. I wondered how we were able to survive at all. He kept insisting that the law be respected, but you know how it was in early 1992. I'm just a small pebble in the entire mosaic, but there were Crisis Staffs, the civilian authorities, military security, and you didn't know who was doing what. And in that sort of situation, it was very difficult to enforce the law. And this was a long and difficult process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. These paramilitaries, the crimes that they were committing, were they against all nationalities, whether Serbs or non-Serbs, or were they limited to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the beginning of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These paramilitaries who you've told us were criminals, were the crimes that they committed against all nationalities or simply against those who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure they committed crimes against all nationalities. I have to illustrate with another example. When I was in Skelani -- when I was in Skelani, the man in whose house I spent the night told me I shouldn't go out at night because I would be killed by someone. There was a paramilitary group active in the area. A man went out to create order. He was a politician, and he was very naive. He tried to remove this renegade check-point at the bridge in Skelani, and they beat the living daylights out of him. Whoever stood in their way would get killed. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Can we just look at a couple of other things in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page in English, and I think it's still the same -- yes, same page in B/C/S. Yeah, sorry, it's the next page in B/C/S as well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph at the top of the page in B/C/S, but the second paragraph in English: "The chief and commander in CSB Pale informed me that about 20 Arkan's men were staying in their area ... in the 'Panorama' Hotel, and they would discuss with them leaving the area of Pale, and they were convinced there shouldn't be any problems about it." Were you aware of Arkan's men staying in the Panorama?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. I do know, however, and this is something characteristic of that paramilitary unit, they were all neat and tidy and disciplined. Some of them may have represented themselves as Arkan's men because Arkan was a name that inspired awe at that time. I don't know whether they were actually Arkan's men or not, the people in Panorama, but I know in other areas units would represent themselves as Arkan's men. And they all had false names. They acted in secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, please, on this report, could we go to the fourth page in English, and in B/C/S it's the next page, dealing with Vlasenica again. In Vlasenica it says: "There are 16 active and 70 reserve policemen. There's a special unit with 25 members for which it is already agreed they will be put under the command of the Army of the Serbian Republic." This is a special unit of the police, is it, they're talking about, the inspector's talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like the situation we discussed yesterday. For example, the Ilijas special unit. But what it says here about the Vlasenica area shows only the continuous attempts to introduce order, because, you see, bringing the reserve force up to manpower level, well, we would know how many policemen and reserve policemen a certain area had to have in proportion to the population. But during the war, the numbers burgeoned. People would come and report to the police stations, and some sort of order had to be introduced. The regulations had to be respected. I don't know what the standards were exactly, the norms, but per thousand inhabitants there would have to be a certain number of police officers, and we tried to act in accordance with those regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Borovcanin, my simple question was are we talking about a special unit of the police, because it just says "special unit"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, it goes on to say, however: "Finally, taking into account the specificity of the area, I suggest that an intervention group should be formed within the SJBs duty service or the police station." Now, isn't an intervention group effectively the same as a Special Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the lines were very fuzzy. You know who a Special was. He was a man who had to have training for all sorts of situations, from rock climbing to diving and so on. Someone can declare themselves to be a Special, a member of a Special Police Unit, but it was far from reality, especially in police stations where there was combat on a daily basis, where the situation was very volatile. All sorts of units would spring up. Some would call themselves a guard. There were lots of paramilitaries in the area. And in May and April, there was general chaos. We couldn't know who was establishing what sort of unit, what the quality of the men was, whether they were qualified to be members of the MUP. That's what the situation was like. These units did exist, there's no doubt about that, but we attempted to introduce some sort of order into all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So the -- sorry, but this report's dated August, but this special unit, which it's agreed they'll put under the command of the Army of the Serbian Republic, is this right, from what you're saying, was not an authorised special unit, which is why the author was suggesting there should be an intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean authorised? Authorised officers were only professional policemen who were employed full time. They were authorised officers. A reserve officer did not have an official ID, did not have -- he could not be an authorised officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right. I'd forgotten about the specific meaning of "authorised." This special unit had not been set up with the authority of the minister or anyone else, had it, because that's why they're being sent to the Army of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. That's all I want to ask you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look next, please, at document 2398. Oh, no, sorry. It's not 2398, is it? Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last report mentioned that you would be doing the report on Bratunac and Skelani, and if we go to the last page in both, we can see that this is your report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, as we can see, if we go back, please, to the first page in each, you carried out the inspection from the 1st to the 3rd of August. And in paragraph beginning "The police officers are mainly engaged on the front lines ..." which we can see halfway down the page, and it's -- it's the penultimate paragraph there. "Lately, a great deal of police officers are engaged in cleaning the ground from Muslim extremists." What are you describing as "Muslim extremists"? Who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, combat activities were very frequent there in that part of the Bratunac municipality, and policemen had no choice but to be actively involved in protecting the citizens in rural areas, in villages, to prevent crimes, because great crimes had been committed in the past there, precisely where you see the reference to the police station in Kravica. There were many other villages and hamlets that were targeted throughout the war. Sometimes those were incursions by sabotage groups and suchlike. So the police had no choice but to get involved in that kind of work to protect the citizens and their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I simply want to know, sorry, sir, who do you mean by "Muslim extremists"? Do you mean the army? Do you mean paramilitary forces? Do you mean ordinary Muslim citizens protecting their homes? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, imagine a group of people which bursts in, killings 11 policemen, and douses them in petrol. Is that a normal soldier? What would you call him? A criminal, war criminal, what? We were afraid of them. And these investigations are still going on, and one day the truth will emerge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So by "Muslim extremists ," you mean criminals, murderers of Muslim nationality? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the precise composition of those groups and what profiles these people were. I don't want to make any claims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but you -- the suggestion in this report is that there are a number of these groups, aren't there, because you say "a great deal of police officers are engaged in cleaning the ground from Muslim extremists"? So you're not talking about one isolated incident there, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, imagine a police station with 20 active-duty and 20 reserve policemen and their rural area is forbidding, villages and hamlets scattered all about, difficult to defend. That's how you should understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well -- and then the remainder of this report deals really with the problem, does it not, of the paramilitary formations that were in both of these municipalities? That's right, isn't it? Both of these police stations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's all I want to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just put an additional question in relation to this report, sir, because I was wondering whether the police officers to whom you refer in the part that has been read out to you by Ms. Korner, whether these police officers were under the command of the police chief at the SJBs involved, or whether these police officers had been resubordinated to the army. Do you understand my question? You say in the report that: "Lately, a great deal of police officers are engaged in cleaning the ground from Muslim extremists." Now, Ms. Korner has clarified what you meant by the expression "Muslim extremists," but my question goes to whether these police officers, during those cleaning operations, had been resubordinated to the army or whether they were acting under the command of the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that they did, in part, act together with the army but sometimes also independently. Why? Sometimes an attack would happen, and there's no -- not much time to report it, to send a dispatch. And by the time you get a feedback, many ugly things could happen in between. So there were no -- there was not time for -- for the usual steps, reporting, approval, et cetera. The command would say, "This is critical line here. You have to send me 10, 15 men, whatever you can spare." And that's -- that's an actual situation. Sometimes, out of necessities, you couldn't go through all the formalities of seeking approvals, et cetera. That is the real take on the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, sir, and I realise that the situation must have been extremely difficult for all parties involved, but from -- you may see -- you may, perhaps, think that this is an overly legalistic question, but I'm interested in clarifying whether the police officers during those cleaning operations were acting under the command of an army officer who was present in the area and governing the activities of the VRS or whether the police officers were acting under the command of the local chief of the SJB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's try to clear that up too. I'm sure, since the military command at in that area was at brigade level, they were much more numerous, they were on the defence line all the time. There was combat nonstop. And whenever police was asked to join them, they were -- they were certainly under military command. You couldn't go solo there. How would the policeman know the situation on the ground unless they reported to the military command to find out and to be assigned somewhere. So that was clear co-operation with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that this is a way in which things should be done, but as we all know, this was not always the way that life played out in practice. So my question is whether police units would occasionally would engage -- would engage themselves in a cleaning operation under their own command. Maybe they would report to the local army officer that they now intended to clean this area, but -- but they were acting during such a cleaning operation under the command of the local SJB chief or somebody else representing the MUP. Did that ever occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the general answer to that question is no. Definitely they would always be in co-ordinated action with the army. Whether someone ever took it upon themselves to go solo and play Rambo, I don't know. The best way to act was to be in co-operation with the army, because then they would have communications, medical services, logistics, et cetera. And plus what could you do with a small group of men, unless they had happened upon a crime in a hamlet and reacted immediately, impromptu. That I cannot say, but normally not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just, again, continue on -- on the theme raised by Judge Harhoff. Co-operation with the army is different, isn't it, from the resubordination you've described which comes as a result of a request and then an order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean different? Maybe you can expand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Where you talked about the operation, and we'll see in the next document I want you to have a look at, it's not the same, is it, as where the army takes over a unit at its request of police, an order is issued, and then the police officers are, as it were, for these purposes, part of the Serbian Army. What you're talking about and what your report is talking about is the police co-operating in the sense of helping, as you put it, get rid of Muslim extremists. "Mopping up," I think, is another term.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. "Co-operation" is a broader term than "co-ordinated action." Co-operation can be an everyday exchange of information, meeting, et cetera, whereas co-ordinated action is something different. For instance, one police unit is engaged within the area of one military command on the ground. Maybe this term "cleaning" or "mopping up" is an unfortunate choice, but even that would fall under the narrow definition of co-ordinated action. That term cropped up in the war. When you are capturing a part of the territory, you have to take all of it. It can't be a leopard skin. It's the doctrine shared by every army in the world. The demarcation lines moved all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if the army, for example, had been carrying out an action somewhere within your territory and had got -- moved on and the police came in, and when I say "mopped up," I use it in it's ordinary sense of arresting people, tightening the -- establishing the security in the area, that would still leave, would it, the police under its own chain of command as opposed to the army chain of command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. You -- you're talking about arrests. Who would you arrest during a military operation unless you are taking -- capturing a part of the territory and then there are some prisoners taken? Otherwise, there's no logic to making arrests. Let's go back to this "mopping up," this unfortunate term. It's just a small part of co-ordinated action in a certain territory, because, in practice, the situation on the ground was such that we had no time to -- to establish proper communication with the command. But once communication is established, then we exchange reports, which territory has been captured, how many people were killed, how many were captured. Those who haven't -- people who haven't lived through that find it difficult to understand. But I had many opportunities to -- to see these ugly scenes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, all I'm trying to establish is whether -- if the police officers as you say in your report were carrying out cleansing operations of Muslim extremists, and the incident you described seemed to talked about an ordinary crime where people burst into the police -- burst in, killing 11 people and doused them in petrol. Now, that's what you described as something these officers were doing. That had nothing to do with army operations, had it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you understood me properly. I mentioned an indent in a different context when 11 of our policemen were ambushed and killed. They were doused in petrol and set on fire. I gave you an example for you to understand what kind of people we were fighting. Of course, normal servicemen would not do something like that. These people, the assailants, must have been sick. And I was the one who collected the victims. I saw that with my own eyes. We had to identify the bodies by their teeth. I couldn't eat for three days after that. I'm talking about that as an inhumane act, something I'm trying to forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction for the transcript. He said "These people, they are extremists, these assailants." "They are extremists." And that part is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, one last try at this. When you wrote this report and you said - and I better go back to it because I'd moved on already. There it is. "... a great deal of police officers are engaged in cleaning the ground from Muslim extremists." Just tell us, one more time, what did you mean they were doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've discuss the matter. Mopping up or cleaning the ground means securing one locality from further incursions by such groups. Let me try to make it clear to you from the military point of view. There is a skirmish, for instance. Somewhere around there is a group that had not had time to withdraw in time, and the skirmish is still going on. Who will attack who first? Now, if the policeman from the next shift comes to the line, he has to be secure. He has to know that his back is safe, that he won't be ambushed again, that that part of the territory is now safe. That's what cleaning the terrain meant, from these pockets, these groups that were still shooting here and there. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you're not talking about the police in this -- being resubordinated to the military. You're talking about police officers acting as police officers. That's what the report says. Because you actually, in the next line, distinguish between the engagement of the police on the front lines and in cleaning the grounds. So there's a difference, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then that's my omission if I didn't stress it. You know, you can't be focused all the time, especially at that time to -- it was difficult to put it all on paper and include everything. I know that you are looking at the legal side, but my side was closer to life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not looking at the legal side at all, sir. All right. Just one other question, please. This incident you described of the police officers who were ambushed and set on fire, can you tell us when that happened, as you remember it so vividly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't forget a thing like that, and time does nothing for it. At that time, the police were supposed to go into --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, sorry, sir. I just want to know the date, the month and the year and the place where this happened.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in Skelani municipality. That is in Podrinje. I forgot the place. Oh, it's Kragivode. It's a village road that goes through the woods. And these 11 policemen were ambushed. They were shot at at the same time from two areas. It was a very clever ambush. None of them had time to react. And then they were doused in petrol and set on fire. It was in Skelani --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us. You told us. I just want the date, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: April. I can't tell you the exact date. April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1993. I see. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- if I may. Witness, sir, still about cleaning the grounds from Muslim extremists, in the beginning when you were telling us about this you said that this was done to protect rural citizens. Could you clarify that for me? What rural citizens? Let's -- would that be Serbian hamlets or Muslim hamlets, or would it make no difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were villages and hamlets populated mainly by Serbs. I can't tell you the exact statistics. Maybe there were some mixed villages. But when the war broke out, everyone who was smart enough left the area of their own will. And even if there had been any Muslims, they might have left before the war, too, but I'm not sure. Some of these villages were ethnically purely Serb. But if police had information that a village was in danger, whether they had received the report from the military commander or some other source, they would have come out to prevent crimes that had already happened before in that area oftentimes, and, of course, there is appropriate documentation. There's no question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when you said that it's normal in any war that when you take a territory you take it all, am I to understand that when you say "cleaning the grounds from Muslim extremists" means removing all Muslims from a territory you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not the way I see it, and that's not the way I explained it. When I say "mopping up," I mean in the course of a military operation. Small pockets of enemy forces were still active, were still firing. It's in that sense that we tried to reinforce the line and protect our own forces, remove those pockets. It was a purely military confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's all I ask on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, it's time for the break. We will resume in -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this document an exhibit? No it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been given the depressing news by the Court Officer that I've only got five minutes left of my original three hours. So could I ask for the extra hour I asked for yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Your Honours, if we are going to be depressed the same way as Ms. Korner, we could also rely, on, I believe, your gratitude sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will consider your application at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, I thought we'd left the document, but I'm afraid over the break I've had an opportunity to think a bit more. Firstly, when I asked you to describe what you were talking about in respect of the term "Muslim extremists," the incident you described happened in 1993, but this report is August 1992. What incidents come to mind, if any, in August of -- up until August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to events that had already taken place against the civilian population, war crimes, slaughtered bodies, and so on. I don't know what normal person could do that, slaughter someone so as to make the corpse unrecognisable. Only extremists can do that. I illustrated this with an example from 1993, but those were the kinds of things that happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but can you think of any particular incident that led you to talk in your report about Muslim extremists in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, can I just say my screen's gone blank in front of me. I don't know if somebody can get a technician.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a very long time ago. If you're thinking of an isolated incident, a specific incident, I can't recall any such thing at the moment. But such crimes did happen, and that is the explanation of the term I used, "extremists."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next thing, you told us that you personally went to inspect this scene. You told us earlier that it wasn't your job to inspect the scene; that was for the crime police. Why were you going down in 1993 to inspect the scene?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I happened to be on the ground. I was a commanding officer at the time, and I spent some 20 or so days in the area, and while I was there, the incident happened, the ambush I mentioned occurred. I happened to be in the vicinity, and I carried out the on-site investigation with a representative of the crime prevention department, and this man was unfortunately killed a year later in an ambush. So we did the inspection together, and we had to inform the families and so on, because there were all sorts of rumours going round that they had been tortured and so on. So we went to document this on the spot, on site, and you can find the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that topic of the crime police, in fact, where there was a crime scene, the area was secured by the uniformed police, wasn't it, as in everybody else's jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, to go back to this incident, it happen in the depth of the territory -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Not the incident. Generally speaking. If a crime was being committed and was being investigated, was it the uniformed police who secured the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The crime prevention department collected traces and clues, photographed the scene, and did everything else that belongs to the investigation, whereas the uniformed police secured the site. This would be a broader area covering one, two, or three villages, and the police would secure the area while the inspection was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was the uniformed police that came within your jurisdiction; is that right? Because that's what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally this on this particular aspect: This report that you wrote or your inspectors wrote, was that given to the chief of the CSB, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. We were always duty-bound to report to our superior officers in the MUP and in the centre. We had instructions on urgent ongoing and interim reporting which regulated all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm going to pause while they check to see why my screen's not working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And would your reports be included in the monthly reports that the CSB was obliged to send to the -- the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just mentioned the instructions we had on urgent reporting, if there was a murder or something, ongoing or regular reporting, and interim reporting when an analysis was being carried out. And all this is prescribed in detail in the instructions. And, of course, we followed those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's all I do ask on that particular aspect. Now could you have a look, very quickly, please, at the document which is number -- sorry. Yes. 318, 65 ter 318. This is a response from Vlasenica SJB, dated the 6th of August, to the request that we looked at earlier for information. I don't know what the number is, but it was the document forwarded by the CSB chief of the 25th of July that we looked at, and I think this is a document whose contents you are aware of, is that right, and you know Mane Djuric, the chief of the SJB who signed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at the bottom of the first page in English, and it's the second paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Combat activities of paramilitaries units were not registered in the area of this station, whilst there were several cases of crimes committed by members of the 'Red Berets,' i.e., the unauthorised transit of stolen cars throughout this area."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we need to go to the next page in English. Second page in English, please. No, not in B/C/S, in English. All right. Anyhow, that's what it says. In the light of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you go back to the first page in B/C/S because that's what he's looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the light of everything that we've seen in your reports and that of your inspectors, when you saw this report back in 1992, was it any surprise to you that apparently the only crime that was being reported by the paramilitary group was the theft of cars -- or, sorry, the unauthorised transit of stolen cars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that wasn't the only sort of crime that occurred, but if you look at the heading, it says: "Joint action between the MUP and the army information," and the date is August 1992. So this is a request for information relating exclusively to joint action carried out by the army and the MUP. So what it says here, Red Berets, theft of cars, and so on, the focus was on police activity jointly with the military. Of course other crimes occurred, but they were mentioned in other reports that you have available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to check whether [indiscernible] I want the next document in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you now look, please, at document 3 -- 65 ter 394. Now, this is Pale police station's response to the request again that we looked at earlier today for information about paramilitaries from the CSB, and this has been sent to your centre. It says, re: your document: "In connection with your document number above, we hereby inform you of the following: "a) there were no paramilitary formations on the territory of this SJBs nor are there any now." Now, this is on the 7th of August. On the 3rd of August, we look at the report that says Arkan's men were stationed in the Panorama Hotel in Pale. Now, can you understand how Pale SJB could have put in this response?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's illogical. It was probably an omission by the local commander. Pale were a place through which everybody passed, so I'm really surprised that the local chief didn't mention that here. Maybe they were no longer there at the point in time. This was already in August. But this is certainly an omission, an error by the person who wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this is something like four days after the inspector's report, and this report is denying that there had ever been any paramilitary formations in Pale, if you look at (a). It says: "There were no paramilitary formations ... nor are there any now."

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here in this document. I agree with you. Okay. But my comment on this is that most probably the chief omitted to include the fact that they had been there previously. You can establish that by looking at a number of other documents or other testimonies. I don't wish to speculate whether he simply omitted to mention this. Most probably yes, but I have reservations in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's not an omission, is it? It's an outright lie. Did you point this out to either your chief or to Mr. Stanisic at any of the collegiums?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mention this particular incident, but this was being continuously discussed. I am surprised by this statement here. Well, let's look at it from a different angle. Why would he have a reason to say these people weren't there if they were causing problems? I know that this chief was a very active person, and he wouldn't allow just anyone to wander around his area stealing and looting. I'm really surprised by this. I have no other comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, Pale was where the government was stationed, wasn't it? Mr. Karadzic and all that lot.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The seat of the government was there in the Panorama for a while and then in some improvised sheds where the ministry sat. All the more reason to remove such negative individuals. That's why I'm surprised by this statement that there were no paramilitary formations there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at number (d), please, and then we need to go to the second page in English only. In English only, not in B/C/S. Thank you. 25

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "We had no prisoners brought in by the army, but we had prisoners brought in and guarded by the police. We have no prisoners at the moment, and we have not had any for any while." Now, here there's no question about it. The prisoners are being brought in by the police, not the army. Did you -- yesterday I asked you about the Dom -- the Kulture Dom, Dom Kulture, and you said that you were aware, you had heard that there were prisoners there or there were people being kept there. Were you surprised by item (d)?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I heard about it, but I didn't see those people myself in the period when they were in the Dom Kulture. And this other statement here -- just a moment. I want to be precise. "We had no prisoners brought in by the army, but we did have prisoners brought in and guarded by the police." It's hard for me to comment on what he meant by that, but I can guess that people from the surrounding villages, Bosniaks or Muslims as they were called at the time, would turn up from the combat area and expected police protection, and the police guarded them for a while. That's how I understand this, although I wasn't there when this was going on. And they -- then they would transport them to the demarcation line. That's how I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You understand the word "prisoners" to mean refugees looking for protection? Is that really what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here, prisoners in the military sense. I don't know what the local chief meant when he used the word "prisoner" in this document, but all those who were being escorted or guarded by the police were in some manner, in one way or another, were deprived of their freedom, because imagine if someone had let those people wander around and they might run into some sort of renegade paramilitary group and a crime might occur and then that would be a stain on the police. There may have been military prisoners, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I don't know if you've her the expression, "Pigs may fly," Mr. Borovcanin. Anyhow, that's all I ask on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that marked -- admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose there's a technical -- there could be technical reason why it shouldn't be through this witness, but I see the logic of it, so it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the police chief who signed, that is not a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Could I ask you now, please, to look briefly at document 1573, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pull it down. No, sorry. No, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. This is a -- the -- a report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command, and I accept entirely you wouldn't have seen it before. I want to ask there about one aspect of what's reported under 4, "Morale." The last three sentences of that paragraph: "Paramilitary formations that are still not disarmed are causing big problems, they behave more violently and are arrogant. Disarming these formations will not be possible without armed clashes with them, especially as they are supported and established by certain organs in the local authorities and the police." Now, were you aware from your inspections of the area within this military command of the police supporting and establishing paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here, I'll quote two sentences: "All the more so as they're supported by some organs of the local authorities and the police." This is absolutely not true what it says here, "and the police." I'm sure of that because we never authorised them to act in any way, and I don't know how the military could write something like this. As for the local authorities, I would be speculating if I were to claim that they were the people under whose auspices they were there. People did say that. There were some rumours to that effect going round, but I can't assert that. However, this simply doesn't hold water, no way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you see, we looked earlier at a report relating to -- I've forgotten which SJB it is now, where there was a -- I'm going to say unauthorised, but not officially approved unit of the Special Police who had been taken into the army. Weren't they paramilitaries? Because they were neither police nor army.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't paramilitaries. They were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina a hundred per cent. Most of the paramilitaries were citizens or nationals of another state, which at that time was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, not all -- well, sorry, you're saying paramilitaries were those who were not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm not saying that local paramilitary units could not be established on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Criminals who were under nobody's command, they would also be paramilitaries. But what I'm talking about now is those groups in the area. Ninety-five per cent of them arrived from Serbia, and that should be seen in that context. As for Vlasenica and the other areas you mention, those were local people, reservists. But we've already discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And we can see at the bottom of the document -- in the English it's over the page, but it's dated the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can just pull down, please, the bottom of the -- yes. That's fine. Your Honours, obviously I can't have it admitted, but could I have it marked for identification, and we'll ask for it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, is it? I wasn't going to do ones that have been exhibited. Sorry about that. Can I just check, Your Honour. The next one is exhibited as well, the one I was going to do, but I just want to see if there's anything I needed to ask him. Yes. Very briefly. Could we have a look at a document that has been exhibited, which is another one of the reports, P632.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is another inspection on the 10th of August. In fact, an inspection of the CSB and also the SJB in Ilidza and Vogosca SJB. We can see that in the third paragraph, and it's -- you were involved in it. Yes. It's signed by a Mr. Rade Radovic, chief of the police duties and tasks department. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we just look at one aspect again of this. At Ilidza, there was a discussion about paramilitaries, the bottom of the first page in English --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go to the second -- the second page in English and also the secretary page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph on both pages: "The problem of Special Units in Ilidza will be resolved through an Act of Systemisation, which has been drafted and harmonised at the CSB." What was the problem with the special units in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was similar to the one you mentioned in Vlasenica, but, again, it was specific because the area was surrounded on all sides. Those special units were necessarily established while combat was going on at the police station, at the collegium meetings, when we decided that order should be introduce. As regards these units, we had only a special squad. These were men who had done such work in the former MUP, and we wanted to introduce order into this situation, to have them under only one command and so on. It's a long story, but you can put specific questions to me and I'll do my best to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I've just got one specific question, Mr. Borovcanin, and that's this: Were these Special Police Units out of control and committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the control of the local SJB, if we're talking about police reservists who were attached to them in terms of organisation. But let me remind you, in the former plans that were drawn up regarding the former All People's Defence for some sort of war where we would be attacked from outside, it was envisaged that such units would be established in areas such as Rakovica. That's on the territory of Ilidza and so on. And there were quite a few of reservists who attached themselves to the police station because that was their military deployment there. So that professionals, active-duty policemen, were mixed with them. And they called themselves a Special Police Unit. And they were active in the very beginning, in May when there was fighting going on at Ilidza every day and so on. At that time, we didn't have any sort of communication, not even phone lines. So we were unable to prevent this situation or introduce order there in a timely manner. That's what the situation was like then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're talking about August -- I'll come on to communications. I'm talking about August of 1992. You dealt with this in your interview. You had proper communication by August of 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm aware that we were talking about August, but I was trying to explain how it happened that those units were established. And later on in some 20 or 25 SJBs, we had to go there, inspect the station, see what was going on, and then deal with it. So this was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, I just -- you didn't actually answer the original question I asked. Were you aware that these so-called special units were actually committing crimes, and that's what was meant by the problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And who was the police chief in Ilidza in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know it was Tomislav Kovac in the beginning, but in August was it Budisa Petko? I'm not sure. I've forgotten. I know Tomo Kovac later went on to other posts in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He later became, didn't he, the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at a later stage, but it went gradually. I think he was first assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One other thing on this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the third page in English, and I believe it's also -- no. It's still the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the -- this report is the 10th of August. The report from Pale police station was the 7th of August, and we discussed what was said. And in this report, three days later: "It was stated while inspecting the Pale Public Security Station that a group of Arkan's men are still present at the Panorama Hotel. Chief Koroman presents that as a solved problem because he's expecting their commander in a couple of days with whom he would solve it without a problem." So it does appear, doesn't it, that Mr. Koroman, for whatever reason, was telling lies in his report of the 3rd of -- 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say he was lying. Maybe he just failed to include that they had been captured. I really dare not speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As you touched on it, can we just deal with communications generally. Can you look, please, at document 1859, 65 ter. This is the CSB quarterly report, is it not, to the ministry, dealing with the period July to September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go in English, please, to page 5, and in B/C/S to the fourth page -- no, fifth page as well, although it says 4 at the top. Yes. No. Fifth page, I'm sorry. I want the 4 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
